A.explanation: 20 nm is much smaller than visible wavelengths and is more typical of atomic scales, so it underestimates the allowed maximum bump size.

B.explanation: About 350 nm is just below the shortest visible wavelength of about 400 nm, so bumps of this size are smaller than all visible light wavelengths.

C.explanation: 720 nm is near the long red end of visible light, so it is larger than violet and blue wavelengths and would not be smaller than all visible light.

D.explanation: $5.0\,\mu\text{m} = 5000\,\text{nm}$ is much larger than any visible wavelength of about $400-700\,\text{nm}$.

hints: Recall the approximate wavelength range of visible light in nanometres - violet is near $400\,\text{nm}$ and red is near $700\,\text{nm}$.
The phrase smaller than the wavelength of visible light means smaller than even the shortest visible wavelength to appear smooth to all colours.
Compare each option in $\text{nm}$ with $400\,\text{nm}$ and ask which is the largest value still clearly below it.
walkthrough: Identify the visible light range: approximately $400\,\text{nm}$ for violet to $700\,\text{nm}$ for red.
For the surface to look smooth to all visible light, the bumps must be smaller than the smallest wavelength used, so smaller than about $400\,\text{nm}$.
Convert option D to nanometres: $5.0\,\mu\text{m} = 5.0 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m} = 5000\,\text{nm}$, which is far too large.
Option C at $720\,\text{nm}$ is above the violet and green wavelengths, and option A at $20\,\text{nm}$ is far below the limit, not the maximum.
The largest value still below about $400\,\text{nm}$ is about $350\,\text{nm}$. This is option B.
